title: I lift up my eyes (Psalm 121)
hook: a pilgrim's song: my help comes from the Lord who made heaven and earth

segments.voice: Yesterday, conies on the rocks and a leviathan made to play. Your line was all made in wisdom. Which creature got a second of your attention? Day four hundred thirty-three.

Three times a year, the law of Moses called the people up to Jerusalem for the great feasts. For families far away that meant days on foot. Dusty roads, children on shoulders, old people on donkeys, everyone singing to keep the pace. And the city sits high in the hills, so the last stretch is always uphill. Fifteen psalms in a row, one hundred twenty to one hundred thirty-four, carry the same heading in the King James Bible: A Song of degrees. Songs of going up. Some readers think pilgrims sang them on that road. Today, one of them, sung by someone looking up at the hills ahead.
screen: `THREE FEASTS A YEAR.` → `THE ROAD GOES UPHILL.` → `SONGS OF GOING UP.`

segments.voice: Psalm one hundred twenty-one begins, in the King James Bible: "I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help." It reads like a statement: my help comes from the hills. But the Hebrew can just as easily be read as a question, and many translations print it that way: I lift up my eyes to the hills. Where does my help come from? Why ask? The hills could be lovely, or they could be frightening. Bandits hid in them. Some readers think of hilltop shrines to other gods, offering help of their own. Either way, the pilgrim looks up, and the next line answers: "My help cometh from the LORD, which made heaven and earth." Not from the hills. From the one who made them. Then the voice changes. Someone else seems to answer the pilgrim, maybe a friend on the road, maybe a priest: "He will not suffer thy foot to be moved: he that keepeth thee will not slumber." Suffer means allow. Your foot won't slip on the path. "Behold, he that keepeth Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep." The King James Bible switches between keep and preserve, so the English hides it, but in Hebrew it is one verb, shamar, six times in eight verses. Keep, keep, keep. The one who keeps watches your coming and going, by day and by night. And the last verse: "The LORD shall preserve thy going out and thy coming in from this time forth, and even for evermore." Every door you walk through, out and back. Some Christians pray this psalm before a journey.
screen: `A STATEMENT, OR A QUESTION?` · `NOT FROM THE HILLS` · `HE NEITHER SLUMBERS NOR SLEEPS` · `KEEP, SIX TIMES IN EIGHT VERSES` · then, large: `MY HELP COMETH FROM THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look toward the hills, or the horizon. If you can see far, a skyline, a ridge, the edge of a field, the top of the tallest building nearby, turn toward it now. If you can't, close your eyes and picture the farthest place you've ever looked out over. Lift your eyes slowly, the way the pilgrim did. Let your breathing slow. Ask the pilgrim's question quietly: where does my help come from? If you pray, you can answer with the psalm: my help cometh from the Lord, which made heaven and earth. If you don't, just keep looking, and let the distance do its work. The bell holds the time.
Shamar. Hebrew for one who keeps and watches over, the word repeated six times in Psalm one hundred twenty-one, a pilgrim's song looking up at the hills and asking where help comes from.
Your line: my help comes. Today, every time you walk out a door, and every time you come back in, remember the last verse: your going out and your coming in. Day four hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: Many Christians pray Psalm 121 before a journey, and it is often read at funerals and at services of blessing for travelers, pilgrims and people leaving home.

original.note: Hebrew: one who keeps, guards, watches over. its root appears six times in this eight-verse psalm.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pretty line about mountain views.
what it means: a pilgrim on the road looks up and asks where help comes from, and the answer is the maker of the hills.
what a scholar hears: verse 1 can be read as a question, and the root shamar, keep, appears six times in eight verses.
recall: to lodge, to spend the night

notes: Count of shamar (keep/preserve) forms in Psalm 121: vv. 3, 4, 5, 7 (twice), 8 = six. Confirm.
Reading of 121:1b as a question is widely adopted in modern translations; the KJV renders it as a relative clause. Confirm wording.
Interpretations of the hills (beauty, danger from bandits, hilltop shrines) offered as possibilities.
The change of speaker in v. 3 is a common scholarly observation; script says 'seems to'.
